en: Maṇḍanamiśra:
[The theories of error are] self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti), apprehension of the non-existent (asatkhyāti), non-apprehension (akhyāti), and misapprehension (anyathākhyāti).
Because there is dispute among investigators due to their confusion, that [confusion] is being analyzed.
That which does not exist does not shine forth, like a sky-flower;
therefore, some maintain that the object is the cognition itself appearing in that form. (MVibhr 2)
And as long as it is impossible [for that], let it be completely abandoned;
for the abandonment of the perceived form is not tenable if [the cognition] is erroneous. (MVibhr 3)
And when a subverting factor is postulated by way of subverting only a single part, it is not logical for there to be a subversion of everything; so the experts in logic maintain. (MVibhr 4)
That which appears externally cannot be maintained as being internal;
it is better that it be non-existent, for such [non-existence] is consistent with its being an error. (MVibhr 5)
Error is not [established] by virtue of being internal, but rather it is accepted as non-existent;
therefore, without conceptualizing it as internal, one indeed postulated its non-existence. (MVibhr 6)

The appearance of an internal object as if it were external is not tenable because it would then be impossible for it to be an error; for if that [external appearance] were postulated as being merely non-existent, it would certainly lack any basis in valid cognition.
The non-existence of that which appears as it does must necessarily be conceptualized;
for whether it is included within [the mind] or exists externally, error is not tenable.
If non-apprehension were without distinction, there would be delusion even in deep sleep;
for non-apprehension exists there as well, and non-apprehension is not differentiated [from that state]. (MVibhr 9)
There is no basis for censure here, because the manifestation of what is non-existent is precisely what constitutes error; such would be the case even in the context of correct cognition.
Error without a substratum is not tenable;
for in the case of a dream, error without a substratum is beyond doubt. (MVibhr 11)
If even that which is not present were apprehended as if it were present,
then the non-existence of the non-present would not differ from that of a sky-flower.
For things that have never been experienced before and which exclude one another, there is no manifestation as if they were present, even when they appear in perception. (MVibhr 13)
What reputation can there be for [an object] equal to a sky-flower, since it appears only as formless?
Yet even that [formless thing] is a factor in worldly transaction, because it appears as if possessing form.
Even if [you accept] such a conceptual construction, there is still no avoidance of the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (asatkhyāti).
For is it not the case that the association with another mode of appearance manifests as something truly non-existent? 15.
Therefore, this appearance as possessing form belongs to that which is non-existent, because it must necessarily be postulated and because of the parsimony of such a postulation. (MVibhr 16)

The latent impression (saṃskāra) of prior knowledge of reality, its awakening along with its causes, and the loss [of memory] expressed as "I remember"—these, together with their respective causes, belong to one who possesses the sense faculties. (MVibhr 17)
In cases of error—such as intense passion, death, fainting, grief, disease, and so forth—the mind’s corruption occurs internally even while the sense organs are present. (MVibhr 18)

Among those who advocate annihilationism, there is a frequent conformity to [the view that] conditioned phenomena persist; among the positions of other schools, it is observed that most [of their assertions] are merely conceptual constructions. (MVibhr 19)

Because there is no memory of what occurs at the end of death, which is the severance of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), it is established that what was experienced in another birth is not remembered. ... [omission] ... [omission] ...
[omission] ... MVibhr 21.

The mind, which is the agent of action, is either accompanied by weak mental formations when [the afflictions] are being severed, or it is devoid of them; or else, it is impaired by defects and lacks such applications as the cultivation of resolve.

One who is healthy, free from defects, and refined by meditative concentration and other virtues, is not like one burdened by tasks during the waking state; such a person is the foremost among those who know the way.
There is both a loss of the capacity for the effect due to the impairment of the defects, and yet there is an excess of the effect—oh, what a discernment of logic! (MVibhr 24)

If there were no cognition of distinction, then the figurative usage [of a term] would occur through superimposition, just as one might think "cow" of a Vāhīka; in that case, there would be no conformity with actual experience. (MVibhr 25)
Even non-apprehension (akhyāti) does not follow from cognition,
since the intellect remains established as "this is silver" through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya).
Therefore, it is logically certain that this is indeed an error; it is not tenable for its cause to be established in accordance with consciousness. (MVibhr 27)
Therefore, the knowers of Brahman consider the indeterminability [of ignorance] to be preferable;
otherwise, the very nature of ignorance as ignorance would be lost. (MVibhr 28)
In the case of a sentient being, emptiness is not false; its manifestation is difficult to define.
They describe that ignorance as being inexpressible in terms of existence or non-existence. (MVibhr 29)
The investigation of an object—whether it exists externally or internally—is not tenable regarding any object of cognition, because that [investigation] would result in its destruction. (MVibhr 30)
This proliferation of name-and-form is described as being nothing other than ignorance;
for one who holds that there is the manifestation of one thing as another, there can be no denial of this proliferation.
If there were no manifestation, the world of proliferation would be nothing but emptiness; on what basis could it exist?
It is logical that the non-proliferated appears in the form of the proliferated.
Granted, you may not clearly perceive it yourself because it is not manifest;
however, you cannot superimpose a manifold nature upon that which does not exist, for such a fabrication would be in vain. (MVibhr 33)

For on a funeral pyre of manifold forms, there would indeed be no liberation by virtue of its very nature as phenomenal proliferation; or else, the consequence of impermanence would follow. (MVibhr 34)
In the case of various delusions such as the city of the Gandharvas and the like, the forms of a single unreal cognition clearly manifest. (MVibhr 35)
The nature of the mind is not real, nor are there superimpositions or clear apprehensions in errors; therefore, the transformation [of consciousness] is the view of those who know Brahman.

Because that which is non-existent cannot be manifested and because it would involve a contradiction with consciousness, those who consider themselves clever have declared that error is simply the non-apprehension of the real. (MVibhr 37)
It appears as if contradictory to say that "nothing shines forth," because if it were shining, it would possess form; it cannot be non-existent, for that would contradict consciousness. (MVibhr 38)
For this very reason, the erroneous manifestation (*anyathākhyāti*) of one thing as another is also not tenable;
for it is utterly inconceivable that one thing should manifest while something else is the object of apprehension. (MVibhr 39)
An object of cognition is not established by the mere fact of being a cause, because that [status] also applies to the sense faculty;
an object of cognition is not defined by causality alone. (MVibhr 40)
If cognition appears as something other than the form of its object,
then it would be without an object at all, because it has fallen away from that defining characteristic [of having an object].
And thus, for that [cognition] which has such a nature, there is no determination of the reality of the object;
even if it were dependent, if it lacks a graspable object, it would be non-cognitive. (MVibhr 42)
There is no certainty regarding the present here due to the suspicion that it might be memory;
for the non-apprehension of distinction cannot logically serve as a cause.
Indeed, when the cause is impaired, there is a clear apprehension of its absence;
and because it is not perceived despite effort, there is certainty regarding its non-existence. (MVibhr 45)
Similarity, non-perception, reflection, and so forth, are the awakeners of the seed of memory;
and because of the loss [of the awareness] that "I remember," there generally occurs a perceptual delusion.
Thus ends the prima facie argument.
If [the object] were exclusively existent, what delusion could there be? If it were non-existent, what could be manifested?
Because it conforms to both, the elders accept that manifestation is otherwise [than either]. (MVibhr 47)
Where nothing whatsoever manifests, there is no delusion;
it is just as the state of darkness, like the shadow of the earth, is perceived during deep sleep. (MVibhr 48)

The manifestation of two [aspects] or of one [aspect] is considered an incorrect error (*vibhrama*). In that regard, what is this "incorrectness"? It is a lack of proficiency residing within consciousness. (MVibhr 49)

Now, there is no apprehension of all aspects, nor is there apprehension of any [aspect] whatsoever; likewise, the manifestation of a real entity as something other than those aspects is not admitted. (MVibh 50)
In that case, when an object is situated at a distance or is subtle, there occurs an indistinct perception; either only the general feature is manifested, or else no error is recognized.
Furthermore, no cognition can apprehend an object in its entirety;
otherwise, all cognitions would necessarily result in falsehood. (MVibhr 52)

Therefore, the cognition of a dream is false because it is known not to be occurring [in the present], whereas [the cognition of the waking state] is [considered real] due to the awareness of its occurrence in the present and the superimposition of unity [upon it]. (MVibhr 53)
The cognition of silver here is not false because of the non-apprehension of the distinction;
in the case of the error of recognition, its nature as memory is not perceived.
Because one [of two objects] is distinct, the other is also distinct;
and because there is no distinction from what is directly perceived, an error regarding direct perception is logical.

If there were an error regarding the object of memory due to a lack of discrimination from what was remembered, activity would not be restricted; nor would it be desirable if cognition were otherwise [than as it appears]. (MVibhr 57)
If it is argued that there is no distinction between the visible and the invisible because [the latter] appears as the desired self,
then surely our cognition would not have a contrary object, due to contradiction with actual experience.
And because it is unreliable, the cognition of silver regarding silver is a memory;
for otherwise, one would not fail to act toward a fragment of mother-of-pearl at that time. (MVibhr 59)
If it is argued that the activity toward silver occurs because of its non-proximity, [we reply:
if the non-proximity is not cognized, from what would there be a restriction of activity? (MVibhr 60)
Whatever arises therein is produced by the proximity of those very [causes];
for otherwise, there would be no apprehension of difference and no apprehension of distinction. (MVibhr 61)
If the difference in activity [toward various objects] were due to the non-apprehension of their distinction because of their similarity,
then one would act toward unseen clods of earth and the like as well, due to that lack of distinction.
If that cognition does not exist there [in the shell], then it would not exist even in the fragment of mother-of-pearl;
if, on the other hand, it exists as having a contrary object, how can its nature as a false manifestation be denied? (MVibhr 63)
Because it is not seen, there is no engagement [with it], just as with a piece of mother-of-pearl;
that form by which it is seen is not the cause of engagement. (MVibhr 64)

If it is argued that this [error] arises from a lack of discrimination between what is seen and what is remembered, then let this be examined here: [does it arise] from the cognition of reality, from the non-cognition of reality, or from the cognition of silver? (MVibhr 65)

If [the object] were perceived, activity would occur toward the former [object]; if it were held that the cognition has a contrary object, there would be no distinction between what is seen and what is unseen; and in the latter case, [such a cognition] would not be useful. (MVibhr 66)
For in the system of the Khayoga, those two are indeed conducive to superimposition;
for if [the object] were not seen or not conjoined with the sense organ, there could be no visual error.

If a difference between memory and the result of valid cognition is admitted, then since their respective objects have been distinguished, on what basis could there be non-distinction [between them]? (MVibhr 68)
If memory did not distinguish its own object from another, then upon seeing a common feature, there would either always be memory of something else or constant delusion. (MVibhr 69)

If this [recognition] were not established through the discernment "I remember," then how could there be the notion of a distinction between cognitions—inferred from their results—when there is no difference in those results? (MVibhr 70)
And the cognition "I remember" is said to be distinct from memory;
nor can it be established as separate from the fruit of a means of knowledge (pramāṇa) without that fruit.
If one's own object is not discerned by mindfulness due to a defect of the mind,
then how could there be the delusion of hair and so forth in a healthy mind, as in the case of ophthalmia?
Even in that case, the mind is not corrupted, because it distinguishes between different objects;
for [the notion of] "having been seen" arises from cognition alone, and [attributing it to the mind] would involve unnecessary complexity.
The world says: "Perceiving through the defects of the sense organs, I am awakening and seeing variegated forms such as paintings and lamps. (MVibhr 74)

It is certain that there would be no perception of fixed error resulting from the various defects of the sense faculties, were it not for the operation of those defects in the non-apprehension [of the object]. (MVibhr 75)
Nor is every error necessarily bound to similarity;
for an illusion of yellow is seen in what is white, and an illusion of bitterness in what is sweet. (MVibhr 76)
Furthermore, since that [object] is not reached when there is no activity [of the sense organ], there is no perception of bile [located] beyond it;
for the perception of something extremely close is difficult to achieve, as in the case of collyrium and the like.

Furthermore, errors such as the [perception of] two moons are not produced by the non-discrimination between the activity of the sense organ and the distinct cognitions arising from it; for they are neither perception nor memory. (MVibhr 78)
And if it had a different object, cognition would not be without an object;
for even by way of another form, the sensory cognition of the eye does not take that [other thing] as its object.
The meaning of "object" (ālambana) is the fitness for the conventional usage associated with that [object];
for it has been shown that even for another [thing], it is simply not the case that it is something else. (MVibhr 80)
Likewise, for one seeking silver, there is an engagement with a fragment of mother-of-pearl;
it appears in some way, yet it does not appear absolutely [as it is].

Therefore, that which is not dependent [on other means of knowledge], such as the Veda and so forth, possesses validity because its form is non-deviant; otherwise, it would be a source of shame. (MVibhr 82)
How can that [requirement for external confirmation] be a source of embarrassment for us who maintain that validity is intrinsic?
Even another [philosopher] has accepted the validity of cognition through its non-deviation [from the object]. (MVibhr 83)

Knowing that the status of being a valid means of cognition arises from [the fact of] awakening itself—the established position of the Mīmāṃsakas—the unwise person rejects it through [an argument based on] non-deviation. (MVibhr 84)
If it is argued that there is no deviation from the object, [we reply: it is not cognized by one who lacks cognition;
and because cognition itself is non-deviant, the claim that "it is the cognition of that" is difficult to establish. (MVibhr 85)
The object of worship is non-different from the knowledge of it, whether in that state or otherwise;
for as long as its non-difference is unestablished, it cannot be apprehended as such.
Moreover, non-distinction is also perceived in the form of cognition;
for if there were a false appearance, it would entail a contradiction with that [non-distinction]. (MVibhr 87)
If that were the case, let that [cognition] alone be the cognizer of the object;
for the object does not exist apart from the consciousness that has attained its capacity through that [cognition].
If the removal of invalidity [of a cognition] occurs through the non-perception of deviation, then once deviation has been established, there would be no validity for that cognition. (MVibhr 89)
This [cognition] whose validity is impaired by deviation does not possess validity through non-deviation;
because it deviates, it is not a logical mark (liṅga), just as a sense organ is not one. (MVibhr 90)
That which attains utility by depending upon the knowledge of a relationship, yet is vitiated by deviation (vyabhicāra), would be a cause of doubt. (MVibhr 91)
A means of cognition does not become defective through its deviation [from the object], but rather by its very existence;
for from consciousness there arises the comprehension of the object through its very existence, just as in the case of the sense faculties and so forth. (MVibhr 92)

That which is obtained from this [linga] by virtue of its form, due to the non-deviation of the linga, does not function as a cause for inference preceded by the power of a well-established cognition. (MVibhr 93)
Regarding validity and its absence, there are non-deviation and its opposite; for thus, even non-deviation is described as being due to cognition alone. (MVibhr 94)
"The exclusion [of the reason] follows from the cognition of sublation; thus it possesses the status of being supported by scripture.
If the capacity of cognition is unestablished, how can that unestablished [reason] be a defeater? (MVibhr 95)

Even when [the pervasion] is established, how could one lead to the incapacity of that which has already established its capacity? For is it not the case that when there is deviation, it is recognized as a subverting cognition? (MVibhr 96)
In that case, the validity of the cognition itself would be undermined;
for an object is determined to be exactly as it appears in the form of the cognition. (MVibhr 97)
It is understood that it is precisely because of the cognition of deviation that [the initial cognition] is not accepted as being exactly so;
that subverting cognition is true wherein it is obstructed. (MVibhr 98)
But in other cases, there would be a sublation neither directly nor even by implication;
that [sublation] would be an inference, and its scope would thus be withdrawn. (MVibhr 99)
It is demonstrated in the Bhāṣya that "the cognition of one who is awake does not arise [as false]";
for us, there is no loss of validity merely from the occurrence of a cognition of deviation. (MVibhr 100)
"There is no confidence in that which is deviant...
In all three ways, validity is not impaired by deviation.
It has been stated that non-exclusion (avyatireka) is not the cause of being a means of valid cognition. (MVibhr 102)

If, due to the absence of a [necessary] cause, there were a reversal of the deviation, then that [deviation] would not be attributed even to smoke and the like, because they are non-deviant. (MVibhr 103)
It is accepted that its status as a factor [of enlightenment] exists precisely because it arises from awakening itself;
for indeed, how could there be non-deviation from causes other than that? (MVibhr 104)
No one accepts the validity of a cognition that does not arise;
for even if it is errant, it produces a cognition restricted to a single object. (MVibh 105)
The eye is accepted as a means of valid cognition with respect to a blue object and also with respect to a white one;
furthermore, deviation does not directly destroy its validity. (MVibh 106)
In some cases, when an erroneous cognition has been perceived, a subverting cognition acts as its destroyer;
however, in the case of [the properties] such as "knowability" (prameyatva) and "verticality" (ūrdhvatā), it is the very act of cognition that is determinative.
"It does not exist" is not a valid means of knowledge; furthermore, because of the absence of a logical reason, that [non-existence] does not exist.
And because of the existence of those [objects], the validity of the sense-faculties—which are themselves subject to deviation—is established. (MVibhr 108)
And once [an object] has been determined, the arising of doubt is not logical because of its dual nature;
for even when a post has been ascertained, people do not remain in a state of uncertainty regarding its height. ... [omission] ...
Nor is it the case that, simply because of a determination, there is in reality no determination. (MVibhr 109–110)
Thus, from whatever [source], it would not be so; this is a very well-spoken [verse]:
"Consciousness, by its very arising, is the determiner of suchness. (MVibhr 111)
If it is not so, then its validity cannot arise from anything else either;
for validity and invalidity consist respectively in non-deviation and its opposite.
In the case of "anaṅga" (the bodiless one), their deliberation here is indeed futile;
therefore, because there is deviation from what appears to be a restrictive determination, a thorough investigation is required. (MVibhr 113)
Having introduced [the topic]...
/ Once that has passed, there would be the certainty of the absence of the fruit due to the absence of the cause. (MVibhr 114)
In the absence of defects in the cause, there is the ascertainment of such a manifestation;
however, when the cause depends upon transformation and other factors, the effect is not certain.
Therefore, even if the reason is not defective, there is no clear apprehension or certainty;
direct experience is what must be established, for it cannot be proven by a deviant reason.
The absence of a contrary result is logical because of the absence of its cause; for once [the cause] has ceased, it establishes a contrary effect that was previously joined with it.
The very nature of the defects reaches full manifestation through their excessive activity,
as is observed in the case of the digestive fire in the stomach when it is afflicted by *bhasmaka* (a morbid condition of hypermetabolism).

When the mind is afflicted by desire and so forth, [the self] is perceived as having the nature of memory through the view; this is because it is cognized in a non-primary sense through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya). // MVibhr 119 //
And since that consciousness is one and undivided, which side could it possibly refute?
To say "the void shines forth" is a pair of contradictory claims.
Emptiness should be described as being devoid of form when it is manifested;
for the separation from all forms is what is designated as "the empty. (MVibhr 121)

If one accepts another form [of emptiness], then the cognition of emptiness regarding that [other form] is itself empty; if it is thought that "non-existence appears in the form of existence," [then that too is empty]. (MVibhr 122)
If it is held that even that [emptiness] is merely an appearance otherwise (anyathākhyāti), then these two—emptiness and the nature of non-existence—are not mutually contradictory. (MVibhr 123)
Therefore, its emptiness here consists merely in its not having that [corresponding] place and time;
for if a thing were to appear exactly as it exists, there would be no error. (MVibhr 124)
When things appear as they do not exist, one is not liberated because of the appearance of emptiness;
some say that the specific modes do not manifest from the possessor of those modes.
They appear as such because they are secluded, and they are thus established as being "peaceful.
Others consider this to be the emptiness of that [subject] alone; it is not otherwise, for it is an error [to think so]. (MVibhr 126)
Cognition does not have another object as its basis; without having a real entity as its objective support, it cannot exist.
However, the author of the *Vārttika* himself has described a resolution to this problem here.
Non-existence is not some other entity distinct from existence, because it cannot be defined as such.
It is true that things exist in a certain way, yet they do not appear in that way; this is considered to be delusion.
It is not that it is not perceived in some manner, nor is it perceived as a mere nothingness;
for how could it be unmanifestable, since it appears in that very way? And so it is.
For non-existence is indeed a different state of being (bhāvāntara) depending on a certain perspective;
moreover, in the theory of misapprehension (anyathākhyāti), there is neither a distinct mode nor is it [the object] real.
Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a manifestation of something belonging to one thing as belonging to another, and that [manifestation] is false;
for indeed, the association with another mode of appearance manifests as something non-existent.
The object of cognition does not possess the nature of another;
for here, no conjunction whatsoever between two distinct things appears. (MVibh 132)
The appearance of something as other than itself—that is false when it is an absence;
for the cognition apprehending an absence relies upon another positive entity. (MVibhr 133)

Apart from that [other entity], nothing indefinable exists as something distinct; therefore, since no non-existence can be established there apart from another entity, [non-existence is not a separate reality]. (MVibhr 134)
The wise do not hold that the emptiness of existence is unreal through cognition;
for even in the case of a hare's horn, there is no such thing as a "nameless" state when it is being manifested.
For in that case, a horn associated with a rabbit is understood;
yet that is not a real entity, since it is not observed in a substrate possessing [real] hooves.
The appearance of that which is non-existent as being unmixed with reality is false; such a cognition is like the perception of a herd of elephants at the tip of a finger. (MV 1.137)
Even in a dream, there is the apprehension of that which is not present as if it were present;
yet there is no lack of distinction from a sky-flower, for its status as a real entity exists at its own time.
For at that very time, the object of knowledge is indeed the cognition itself;
here, even its "presentness" is perceived, while elsewhere it is merely conceptualized.
Even for others who hold mutually contradictory views, there exists the state of being absolutely unperceived [by one another], because it is produced by that [very fact]. (MVibhr 140)

Consciousness is not empty of the object of knowledge, because that would entail the loss of its own nature; for [consciousness] would then be joined with a non-entity, and the mind would lack autonomy. (MVibhr 141)
Even very many unseen things are postulated provided they possess valid means of cognition;
however, the true nature of the causes for the cessation of conditioned formations is not established with absolute certainty.
It is established that what was experienced in another birth is not remembered;
yet they claim to perceive the connection between that action and its fruit. (MVibhr 143)
For in this way, even one who remembers the various types of karma within beginningless saṃsāra—who, because of the infinity of karma performed, could know whose what fruit is? (MVibhr 144)
In a dream, the disturbance of the internal mind awakens the seed of memory;
however, because that [disturbance] is absent for one who is awake, the vision of a dream does not arise.
Even when there is an affliction by desire and so forth, a preponderance of activity is likewise illustrated:
for this [mind] grasps that which is indeed ungraspable and itself imagines it.
That [cognition] is produced by a mind whose defects have been diminished;
it is not metaphorical (gauṇī), because it is determined as such through superimposition (adhyāropa). (MVibhr 147)
When it is present, that which is non-empty appears as something real, struck by another entity;
however, its non-existence does not shine forth, for that [non-existence] is not empty because it lacks self-nature.
In this way, ignorance cannot be dismissed as something that can be defined, because if it were anything other than ignorance, it would manifest the nature of another thing.
The falsity of a cognition that is sublated cannot be established otherwise;
therefore, it is logical that as long as something is subject to sublation, it is false. (MVibhr 154)

Regarding the object of error, its externality is not negated by subverting arguments; nor is it understood as being internal, nor is there a cognition [of it] through its being inexpressible. (MVibhr 155)
However, what is perceived is that the external object does not exist at that place and time;
therefore, it is not the case that the external object is unreal, because it is not sublated by cognition.

Sublation, which consists in the negation of what has been apprehended, is not tenable if there is no manifestation [of error]; moreover, for us, sublation itself clearly establishes that there is a manifestation of something other [than reality]. (MVibhr 157)
For non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) is not tenable as a reductio (*prasañjikā*) in our position;
nor is this a negation of apprehension, because that would entail the consequence of [all] cognition being [non-apprehensive]. (MVibhr 158)
This negation based on discrimination is not apprehended through perception;
such a cognition of discrimination does not occur either successively or simultaneously. (MVibhr 159)

If it were the case that there is grasping due to non-discrimination, but not [grasping] of two distinct things, then since there is no attainment when there is no grasping, it is logical that [discrimination] occurs prior to attainment. ... [omission] ...
Furthermore, since both [subject and object] are absent in a dream, of what two things could discrimination be perceived?
If [the cognition] is not distinct because it is remembered, then such sublation would be thwarted;
likewise, every such sublation would subsequently be a cognition of a property in a subject. (MVibhr 162)
Therefore, this argument would be appropriate [only] if there were a subverting cognition;
for even if the object exists otherwise, this form is perceived by the cognition. (MVibh 163)
In the theory of self-manifestation (*ātmakhyāti*), some say that everything is internal; in the theory of the manifestation of emptiness (*śūnyakhyāti*), they say it is only empty.
In the theory of non-manifestation (*akhyāti*), there is no distinction between the real and the false; therefore, this is the differentiation among these types of errors. (MVibhr 164)
